claim: A high density of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) is associated with poorer prognosis and survival in breast cancer patients.
source: A high density of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) is associated with poorer prognosis and survival in breast cancer patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature as indicated in the abstract.

claim: Lipid accumulation in TAMs can promote tumor growth and metastasis in various models.
source: Recent studies have shown that lipid accumulation in TAMs can promote tumor growth and metastasis in various models.
evidence: This claim references recent studies, indicating citation-based support.

claim: Unsaturated fatty acids are more likely to form lipid droplets in murine macrophages than saturated fatty acids.
source: Herein, we demonstrated that unsaturated fatty acids (FAs), unlike saturated ones, are more likely to form lipid droplets in murine macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential lipid droplet formation.

claim: Unsaturated FAs, including linoleic acids (LA), activate the FABP4/CEBPα pathway, leading to triglyceride synthesis and lipid droplet formation.
source: Specifically, unsaturated FAs, including linoleic acids (LA), activate the FABP4/CEBPα pathway, leading to triglyceride synthesis and lipid droplet formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing pathway activation and lipid droplet formation.

claim: FABP4 enhances lipolysis and FA utilization by breast cancer cell lines, which promotes cancer cell migration in vitro and metastasis in vivo.
source: Furthermore, FABP4 enhances lipolysis and FA utilization by breast cancer cell lines, which promotes cancer cell migration in vitro and metastasis in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro migration assays and in vivo metastasis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A deficiency of FABP4 in murine macrophages significantly reduces LA-induced lipid metabolism.
source: Notably, a deficiency of FABP4 in murine macrophages significantly reduces LA-induced lipid metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing FABP4 WT and KO macrophages.

claim: FABP4 is a crucial lipid messenger that facilitates unsaturated FA-mediated lipid accumulation and lipolysis in TAMs, thus contributing to the metastasis of breast cancer.
source: Therefore, our findings suggest FABP4 as a crucial lipid messenger that facilitates unsaturated FA-mediated lipid accumulation and lipolysis in TAMs, thus contributing to the metastasis of breast cancer.
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Macrophages are present in almost all tissues of an organism, where they play pivotal roles in maintaining tissue homeostasis or contributing to disease pathogenesis.
source: As a main arm of innate immunity, macrophages are present in almost all tissues of an organism, where they play pivotal roles in maintaining tissue homeostasis or contributing to disease pathogenesis (Jin et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TAMs are the most abundant immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), actively participating in tumor progression and metastasis.
source: In breast cancer, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are the most abundant immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), actively participating in tumor progression and metastasis (Pollard, 2004; Condeelis and Pollard, 2006; Allison et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A high presence of TAMs in the TME correlates with a poorer prognosis of cancer patients in clinical studies.
source: A high presence of TAMs in the TME correlates with a poorer prognosis of cancer patients in clinical studies (Finak et al., 2008; Beck et al., 2009; Mehta et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Macrophage deletion via genetic or therapeutic approaches results in inhibition and regression of mammary tumors in pre-clinical studies.
source: Moreover, macrophage deletion via genetic or therapeutic approaches results in inhibition and regression of mammary tumors in pre-clinical studies (Luo et al., 2006; Galmbacher et al., 2010; Linde et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pre-clinical studies.

claim: Macrophages are known for their heterogeneity regarding origin, phenotypes, and functional states.
source: Macrophages are known for their heterogeneity regarding origin, phenotypes, and functional states (Gordon and Taylor, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In response to diverse environmental stimuli from the environment, macrophages are believed to acquire a spectrum of functional states in vivo.
source: In response to diverse environmental stimuli from the environment, macrophages are believed to acquire a spectrum of functional states in vivo (Stout and Suttles, 2004; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Macrophages are commonly divided into the M1/M2 paradigm based on the concept of adaptive Th1/Th2 polarization.
source: To understand their functional versatility, macrophages are commonly divided into the M1/M2 paradigm based on the concept of adaptive Th1/Th2 polarization (Martinez et al., 2009; Mosser and Edwards, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Th1-derived cytokines polarize macrophages to M1 phenotype, which express inducible nitric oxide synthase and exhibit anti-tumor activities.
source: Generally, Th1-derived cytokines polarize macrophages to M1 phenotype, which express inducible nitric oxide synthase and exhibit anti-tumor activities.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about macrophage polarization.

claim: Th2-cytokines polarized M2 macrophages highly express arginase 1, CD206, VEGFs, IL-10, TGFβ, etc., supporting angiogenesis and favoring tumor growth.
source: Th2-cytokines polarized M2 macrophages highly express arginase 1, CD206, VEGFs, IL-10, TGFβ, etc., supporting angiogenesis and favoring tumor growth (Mantovani and Sica, 2010; Sica et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The M1/M2 classification is likely oversimplified given the complex functional states of macrophages in vivo.
source: However, given the complex functional states of macrophages in vivo (Murray et al., 2014), the M1/M2 classification is likely oversimplified.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TAMs do not follow the two extreme M1/M2 activation states in vivo.
source: Many studies demonstrate that TAMs do not follow the two extreme M1/M2 activation states in vivo (Hao et al., 2018a; Weiss et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Macrophage metabolism determines their functional outcome.
source: There is a growing realization that macrophage metabolism determines their functional outcome (Ip et al., 2017; O'Neill and Pearce, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lipid accumulation in TAMs promotes tumor growth and metastasis in multiple cancer models, including breast cancer.
source: Several recent studies in multiple cancer models, including breast cancer (Huggins et al., 2021; Masetti et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019), reported that lipid accumulation in TAMs promotes tumor growth and metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Lipid accumulation promoted the expression of Arg1, VEGFα, MMP9, IL-6, PD-L1, CCL-6, etc., thus conferring TAMs with immune suppressive and pro-tumorigenic phenotypes.
source: Specifically, lipid accumulation promoted the expression of Arg1, VEGFα, MMP9, IL-6, PD-L1, CCL-6, etc., thus conferring TAMs with immune suppressive and pro-tumorigenic phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from cited studies.

claim: Lipid droplet formation was a characteristic feature of the pro-tumor TAMs.
source: Lipid droplet formation was as a characteristic feature of the pro-tumor TAMs, but the underlying molecular mechanisms driving lipid droplet formation in TAMs remain to be determined.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the literature.

claim: Lipid droplets are all formed by a phospholipid monolayer enclosing a neutral lipid core.
source: Despite morphological and compositional differences, lipid droplets are all formed by a phospholipid monolayer enclosing a neutral lipid core (Olzmann and Carvalho, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A key step of lipid droplet formation is to synthesize neutral triacylglycerol (TAG), which requires the esterification of activated fatty acids (FA) to diacylglycerol (DAG).
source: A key step of lipid droplet formation is to synthesize neutral triacylglycerol (TAG), which requires the esterification of activated fatty acids (FA) to diacylglycerol (DAG) (Tauchi-Sato et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Enzymes including glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT), acyl-CoA:1-acyl-glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (AGPAT), DAG acyltransferases (DGATs), are key in the biogenesis of neutral lipids.
source: During this step, enzymes including glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT), acyl-CoA:1-acyl-glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (AGPAT), DAG acyltransferases (DGATs), are key in the biogenesis of neutral lipids.
evidence: This claim is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Fatty acid binding proteins (FABPs) have evolved to solubilize FAs, facilitating their transport and responses.
source: Due to the insolubility of hydrophobic FAs, fatty acid binding proteins (FABPs) have evolved to solubilize FAs, facilitating their transport and responses (Furuhashi and Hotamisligil, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: FABP4 is the most well studied among FABPs given its striking biology in regulating macrophage lipid metabolism and functions in multiple disease settings.
source: Among FABPs, adipose FABP (A-FABP or FABP4) is the most well studied given its striking biology in regulating macrophage lipid metabolism and functions in multiple disease settings (Jin et al., 2021a; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A subset of macrophages with the phenotype of CD11b+F4/80+Ly6C-CD11c-MHCII- highly express FABP4, facilitating macrophage lipid processing and patrolling functions.
source: Our pre-clinical studies demonstrated that a subset of macrophages with the phenotype of CD11b+F4/80+Ly6C-CD11c-MHCII- highly express FABP4, facilitating macrophage lipid processing and patrolling functions (Jin et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2017c).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous studies.

claim: FABP4 was identified as a functional marker for protumor TAMs by enhancing the oncogenic IL-6/STAT3 signaling.
source: Moreover, FABP4 was identified as a functional marker for protumor TAMs by enhancing the oncogenic IL-6/STAT3 signaling (Hao et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All the FAs studied (PA, SA, OA, LA) were oxidized by mitochondria as evidenced by the increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) when compared to the BSA control.
source: Using a macrophage cell line, we demonstrated that all the FAs studied were oxidized by mitochondria as evidenced by the increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) when compared to the bovine serum albumin (BSA) control (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Saturated FAs increase lysosome contents in macrophages.
source: Interestingly, when measuring their impact on other cellular organelles, FAs exhibited dichotomous effects, with saturated FAs increasing lysosome contents (Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Unsaturated FAs promote ER formation in macrophages.
source: while unsaturated FAs promoting ER (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Unsaturated FAs dramatically promote lipid droplet (LD) formation in macrophages.
source: and, more dramatically, lipid droplet (LD) formation (Figure 1E) in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Unlike saturated FA, unsaturated FA significantly induced LD formation in primary peritoneal macrophages and bone-marrow-derived macrophages.
source: Using primary peritoneal macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and bone-marrow-derived macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), we observed the similar phenomenon that unlike saturated FA, unsaturated FA significantly induced LD formation in these macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Oil Red O staining confirmed the presence of LD formation.
source: Oil Red O staining confirmed the presence of LD formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The observation of unsaturated FA-induced LD formation in macrophages was consistent regardless of FA concentrations and treatment durations.
source: Of note, the observation of unsaturated FA-induced LD formation in macrophages was consistent regardless of FA concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and treatment durations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claim: OA/LA-induced LD accumulation was not associated with the lysosome, but colocalized in the ER.
source: With a multispectral imaging analysis, we demonstrated that OA/LA-induced LD accumulation was not associated with the lysosome, but colocalized in the ER (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by multispectral imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: OA and LA specifically induced LD formation in the cytoplasm.
source: Transmission electron microscope further confirmed that OA and LA specifically induced LD formation in the cytoplasm (Figure 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscope data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: LA-induced lipid droplets were formed in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in macrophages.
source: which were bud from ER (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Unsaturated FA-induced LD biogenesis in macrophages mainly occurs in the ER.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that unsaturated FA-induced LD biogenesis in macrophages mainly occurs in the ER.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing ER colocalization and budding.

claim: PA or LA treatment had similar effects on Acs1, Cpt1a, Cpt1b, HMGCR, Acat1, and Acat2 expression in macrophages.
source: In response to PA or LA treatment, Acs1, Cpt1a, Cpt1b, HMGCR, Acat1, and Acat2 had similar expression pattern in macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: Both PA and LA exerted similar effects on FA activation, mitochondrial oxidation, cholesterol synthesis and esterification.
source: suggesting that both FA types exerted similar effects on FA activation, mitochondrial oxidation, cholesterol synthesis and esterification.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the similar gene expression patterns observed.

claim: Genes encoding rate-limiting enzymes in TAG synthesis, including Gpam1, Dgat1 and Dgat2, were significantly increased by treatment with LA, but not PA.
source: Interestingly, genes encoding rate-limiting enzymes in TAG synthesis, including Gpam1, Dgat1 and Dgat2, were significantly increased by treatment with LA, but not PA (Figure 2B–H)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2B–H.

claim: LA has a unique role in transcriptional upregulation of neutral lipid synthesis pathways.
source: suggesting a unique role of LA in transcriptional upregulation of neutral lipid synthesis pathways.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential gene expression observed with LA vs PA treatment.

claim: Macrophages treated with LA, but not BSA or PA, exhibited elevated levels of LipidTOX, GPAT1, and DGAT1.
source: We observed by confocal microscopy that macrophages treated with LA, but not BSA or PA, exhibited elevated levels of LipidTOX, GPAT1, and DGAT1 (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: There was a significant increase of lipid accumulation (LipidTOX), GPAT1 and DGAT1 proteins in the LA-treated vs. the BSA or PA groups.
source: Quantitative measurements showed a significant increase of lipid accumulation (LipidTOX), GPAT1 and DGAT1 proteins in the LA-treated vs. the BSA or PA groups (Figure 2J–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J–M.

claim: Unsaturated FAs significantly increased lipid accumulation by enhancing GPAT/DGAT-mediated lipid accumulation in macrophages.
source: Moreover, intracellular flow cytometric staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–I) and quantification by mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–L) also confirmed our observations that unsaturated FAs significantly increased lipid accumulation by enhancing GPAT/DGAT-mediated lipid accumulation in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–L.

claim: C/EBPα and C/EBPβ were predicted to commonly bind the promotor regions of genes related to TAG synthesis pathways.
source: Two transcriptional factors, C/EBPα and C/EBPβ, were predicted to commonly bind the promotor regions of these genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of transcription factor binding sites.

claim: C/EBPα, but not C/EBPβ, was significantly upregulated by LA treatment in macrophages.
source: When macrophages were treated with PA or LA, C/EBPα (Figure 3A), but not C/EBPβ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), was significantly upregulated by LA treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: C/EBPα was mainly localized in the cytosol with BSA and PA treatment but was significantly upregulated in the nuclei with LA treatment.
source: Confocal microscopy showed that C/EBPα was mainly localized in the cytosol with BSA and PA treatment but was significantly upregulated in the nuclei with LA treatment (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: C/EBPβ was present in both cytosol and nuclei regardless of PA or LA treatment.
source: In contrast, C/EBPβ was present in both cytosol and nuclei regardless of PA or LA treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: LA treatment induces specific activation of C/EBPα in macrophages.
source: These results suggest that LA treatment induces specific activation of C/EBPα in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the nuclear localization and upregulation of C/EBPα with LA treatment.

claim: LA-induced gene expression of Gpam1, Dgat1, Dgat2 was abrogated when C/EBPα was silenced.
source: LA-induced gene expression of Gpam1, Dgat1, Dgat2 was abrogated when C/EBPα was silenced (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from C/EBPα knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3E–G.

claim: The uptake of FA (Cd36), lysosome lipase (Lipa) and mitochondrial oxidation (Cpt1b) were significantly increased in C/EBPα-knockdown macrophages.
source: Moreover, the uptake of FA (Cd36), lysosome lipase (Lipa) and mitochondrial oxidation (Cpt1b) were significantly increased in C/EBPα-knockdown macrophages (Figure 3H–J)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3H–J.

claim: C/EBPα knockdown not only inhibited lipid synthesis, but also promoted lipolysis and oxidation.
source: suggesting that C/EBPα knockdown not only inhibited lipid synthesis, but also promoted lipolysis and oxidation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the gene expression changes observed with C/EBPα knockdown.

claim: C/EBPα knockdown significantly inhibited LA-induced neutral lipid accumulation as shown by the staining of BODIPY and Oil Red O in macrophages.
source: As such, C/EBPα knockdown significantly inhibited LA-induced neutral lipid accumulation as shown by the staining of BODIPY (Figure 3K) and Oil Red O (Figure 3L and M) in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by BODIPY and Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 3K, L, and M.

claim: C/EBPβ silencing did not affect the expression of Gpam1, Cd36, and Lipa expression.
source: By contract, C/EBPβ silencing did not affect the expression of Gpam1, Cd36, and Lipa expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data from C/EBPβ knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: C/EBPβ knockdown appeared to inhibit the expression of Dgat1 and Dgat2.
source: Although C/EBPβ knockdown appeared to inhibit the expression of Dgat1 and Dgat2
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression data from C/EBPβ knockdown experiments.

claim: C/EBPβ knockdown also inhibited Cpt1b-mediated FA oxidation.
source: it also inhibited Cpt1b-mediated FA oxidation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I–K.

claim: C/EBPβ knockdown resulted in lipid accumulation in response to LA treatment in macrophages.
source: Overall, C/EBPβ knockdown resulted in lipid accumulation in response to LA treatment in macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipid accumulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: C/EBPα, but not C/EBPβ, is a critical transcriptional factor controlling LA-induced TAG synthesis and LD formation in macrophages.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that C/EBPα, but not C/EBPβ, is a critical transcriptional factor controlling LA-induced TAG synthesis and LD formation in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential effects of C/EBPα and C/EBPβ knockdown on lipid metabolism.

claim: FA treatment mainly induced expression of FABP4, but not FABP3 and FABP5, in macrophages.
source: We measured the profile of common FABP members in macrophages and demonstrated that FA treatment mainly induced expression of FABP4, but not FABP3 and FABP5, in macrophages (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: FABP4 was mostly correlated with C/EPBα compared to other FABP family members in the TCGA human breast cancer database.
source: Analyzing the TCGA human breast cancer database, we found that compared to other FABP family members FABP4 was mostly correlated with C/EPBα (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: FABP4 was not correlated with other C/EBP members in the TCGA human breast cancer database.
source: but not with other C/EBP members (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The positive associations of FABP4 with C/EBPα and key TAG synthesis genes were evidenced in multiple GEO datasets.
source: The positive associations of FABP4 with C/EBPα and key TAG synthesis genes were also evidenced in multiple GEO datasets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GEO datasets shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: FABP4 was enriched in clusters 0, 1, and 2 of splenic macrophages.
source: UMAP plots showed that macrophages consisted of 13 clusters based on untargeted gene expression profiles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G). FABP4 was enriched in clusters 0, 1, and 2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: FABP4 was mainly involved in protein-lipid complex, lipid binding and signaling receptors based on GO molecular function analysis.
source: Compared to other non-enriched clusters (Fabp4-), GO molecular function analysis showed that FABP4 was mainly involved in protein-lipid complex, lipid binding and signaling receptors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Fabp4 enriched clusters (Fabp4+) were highly associated with genes known to be critical for lipid uptake and accumulation, including Cd36, PPARγ, CEBPA, Plin2.
source: Moreover, Fabp4 enriched clusters (Fabp4+) were highly associated with genes known to be critical for lipid uptake and accumulation, including Cd36, PPARγ, CEBPA, Plin2 (Figure 4E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E–I.

claim: Fabp4 enrichment was not related to Fabp5, Acsl1, Lipa, Fasn, and Cpt1b.
source: In contrast, Fabp4 enrichment was not related to Fabp5, Acsl1, Lipa, Fasn, and Cpt1b (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–L)
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–L.

claim: FABP4 has a unique role in lipid uptake and storage in macrophages.
source: suggesting a unique role of FABP4 in lipid uptake and storage in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the gene expression patterns observed in FABP4-enriched clusters.

claim: FABP4 was mainly expressed in the cytosol in BSA- or PA-treated cells, whereas LA treatment led to FABP4 present both in the cytosol and nuclei.
source: Confocal microscopy showed that FABP4 was mainly expressed in the cytosol in BSA- or PA-treated cells, whereas LA treatment led to FABP4 present both in the cytosol and nuclei (Figure 4K)
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: LA treatment induced FABP4 nuclear translocation for potential nuclear transactivation.
source: suggesting a LA-induced FABP4 nuclear translocation effect for potential nuclear transactivation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed nuclear localization of FABP4 with LA treatment.

claim: Deletion of FABP4 in macrophages abrogated LA-induced C/EBPα expression in nuclei.
source: To confirm the role of FABP4, we measured C/EBPα expression in FABP4-deficienct macrophages. Deletion of FABP4 in macrophages abrogated LA-induced C/EBPα expression in nuclei (Figure 4L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy and gene expression data shown in Figure 4L and M.

claim: FABP4 deficiency significantly blocked LA-induced expression of C/EBPα in primary peritoneal macrophages and bone-marrow-derived macrophages.
source: We further confirmed that FABP4 deficiency significantly blocked LA-induced expression of C/EBPα (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M and N), but not C/EBPβ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O and P), in primary peritoneal macrophages and bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M and N.

claim: FABP4 deficiency did not affect LA-induced expression of C/EBPβ in primary peritoneal macrophages and bone-marrow-derived macrophages.
source: We further confirmed that FABP4 deficiency significantly blocked LA-induced expression of C/EBPα (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M and N), but not C/EBPβ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O and P), in primary peritoneal macrophages and bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1O and P.

claim: FABP4 plays a pivotal role in mediating LA-induced C/EBPα activation in macrophages.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrated a pivotal role for FABP4 in mediating LA-induced C/EBPα activation in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing FABP4's role in C/EBPα activation.

claim: Upregulation of Gpam1, Dgat1, and Dgat2 in response to LA treatment in WT macrophages was significantly reduced when FABP4 was genetically depleted.
source: Using FABP4 wild type (WT) and knockout (KO) macrophage cell lines (Figure 5A), we demonstrated that upregulation of Gpam1, Dgat1, and Dgat2, but not Gpam4 and Agpat2, in response to LA treatment in WT macrophages, was significantly reduced when FABP4 was genetically depleted (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5B–F.

claim: FABP4 deficiency did not affect LA-induced upregulation of Gpam4 and Agpat2.
source: we demonstrated that upregulation of Gpam1, Dgat1, and Dgat2, but not Gpam4 and Agpat2, in response to LA treatment in WT macrophages, was significantly reduced when FABP4 was genetically depleted (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5B–F.

claim: FABP4 deficiency significantly reduced the expression of LA-induced Gpam1, Dgat1, Dgat2 in peritoneal macrophages.
source: Similarly, using peritoneal macrophages purified from WT and KO mice, we confirmed that FABP4 deficiency significantly reduced the expression of LA-induced Gpam1, Dgat1, Dgat2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: FABP4 deficiency also reduced expression of other lipid transporters, including Cd36 and Fabp5.
source: Of note, FABP4 deficiency also reduced expression of other lipid transporters, including Cd36 and Fabp5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: FABP4 deficiency results in a general inhibition of fatty acid uptake and metabolism in primary macrophages.
source: suggesting a general inhibition of fatty acid uptake and metabolism in the absence of FABP4 in primary macrophages.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the reduced expression of multiple lipid metabolism genes in FABP4-deficient macrophages.

claim: GPAT1, DGAT1, and lipidTOX were colocalized in the cytoplasm of WT macrophages whereas FABP4 deficiency reduced the expression of GPAT1, DGAT1, and lipidTOX in KO macrophages.
source: Confocal microscopy showed that GPAT1, DGAT1, and lipidTOX were colocalized in the cytoplasm of WT macrophages whereas FABP4 deficiency reduced the expression of GPAT1, DGAT1, and lipidTOX in KO macrophages (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: GPAT1, DGAT1, and lipidTOX levels were significantly reduced when FABP4 was absent.
source: Quantitative analysis demonstrated that GPAT1, DGAT1, and lipidTOX levels were significantly reduced when FABP4 was absent (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: FABP4 deficiency compromised LA- and OA-induced lipid accumulation in macrophages.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy, we further confirmed that FABP4 deficiency compromised LA- and OA-induced lipid accumulation in macrophages (Figure 5L, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: LA-induced neutral lipid accumulation in primary peritoneal macrophages was significantly reduced when FABP4 was deficient.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and I, LA-induced neutral lipid accumulation in macrophages was significantly reduced when FABP4 was deficient.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: FABP4 plays a pivotal role in TAG synthesis and neutral lipid accumulation in macrophages.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that FABP4 plays a pivotal role in TAG synthesis and neutral lipid accumulation in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the multiple lines of evidence showing FABP4's role in lipid metabolism.

claim: FABP4 expression was highly associated with the lipolysis regulation pathway, including genes of β-adrenergic receptors (Adrb2), G-protein-coupled receptor signaling (Adcy4), and lipolysis enzymes (Pnpla2, Lipe) in the TCGA breast cancer datasets.
source: Interestingly, FABP4 expression was highly associated with the lipolysis regulation pathway, including genes of β-adrenergic receptors (Adrb2), G-protein-coupled receptor signaling (Adcy4), and lipolysis enzymes (Pnpla2, Lipe) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: FABP4 deficiency impaired LA-induced lipolysis in macrophages as evidenced by significantly reduced levels of Adrb2, Adcy4, Pnpla2, and Lipe.
